Execution Before Memory:
Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models

Weiyang Jin Affiliation: University of Hong Kong (hku.hk) Affiliation: Equal contribution    Jiwen Yu Affiliation: University of Hong Kong (hku.hk) Affiliation: Equal contribution    Sihan Xu Affiliation: University of Michigan - Ann Arbor (umich.edu)    Yuwei Niu Affiliation: Peking University (pku.edu.cn)    Xihui Liu Affiliation: University of Hong Kong (hku.hk) Affiliation: Corresponding author
Abstract

A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench’s score TT rises by 26.1% and MBench-T’s score UU by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

keywords
video world models, memory evaluation, delayed reveal, test-time revision
Website hku-mmlab.github.io/MIST
Code github.com/HKU-MMLab/MIST

1 Introduction

Memory tests for video world models ask about a scene the camera no longer shows: who sat down, what went into the box, whether the candy broke (Brooks et al., 2024; Bruce and others, 2024; Valevski et al., 2024). Object relations have to survive when the camera looks away, and actions have to update them (Shin et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). Current tests fold these checks into one number: a person and a chair, an object left in a room, or a cube still in a cup (Lu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). A low number is easy to read as forgetting, yet it cannot say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, or whether the last frame shows the result (Fig. 1).

When the change is not carried out, the hidden transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. Figure 2 shows the usual clip. The child never sits before the camera leaves. The camera comes back to candy that was never broken. A box stays shut. The task names the target, but the last frame never shows it. The score drops before memory is tested. Until that change happens, asking the model to remember targets the wrong stage. Tools that rewrite a video for quality, physics, or preference do not ask whether the asked change was shown (Lee et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a). What is needed first is an evaluation that separates the change from its result.

We introduce MIST to separate the two. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. On Wan TI2V-5B, three 5-second shots and 43 cases, the scene is usually set and the hidden change does not leak, yet 41 of 43 baseline clips never show it. Asking only to open leaves most lids down, and naming the answer helps less than revising the failed move (§4). Looking at the last frame and revising the instruction makes the change appear, though the shown state can still be wrong. The bottleneck is therefore execution: the scene is set, but the instructed change is not carried out.

The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. Failed clips on WRBench skip the departure or the return, and failed clips on MBench-T return to an object that is still intact (§7). On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move). It recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the same model carries out the requested instruction. No memory module is added or trained. Relative to the baseline, MIST reveal rises from 0.147 to 0.492. On the benchmarks, WRBench’s score TT rises by 26.1% (0.452→\to0.570, n=40n{=}40) and MBench-T’s score UU by 52.7% (0.292→\to0.446, n=30n{=}30; 23 of 30 keep the baseline).

These results say where the score is lost. They do not show that the model stored the target state. A judged last frame is not stored memory (§8). They do show that the model can already carry out many missing changes once the instruction names them. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can already do once the move is stated.

This paper makes three contributions (Fig. 1). (1) MIST, an evaluation that scores whether the scene is set, whether the hidden change leaks, and whether it is finally shown, so a missing change is not reported as forgetting (§3–4). (2) Evidence that failed official clips also miss the asked change: a skipped return on WRBench, an intact object on MBench-T (§7). (3) M3-Agent, which recursively revises the input instruction on the same model. It more than triples MIST reveal and raises TT by 26.1% and UU by 52.7% (§5, §7).

2 Related Work

A low memory score can come from failed persistence, a wrong state update, or a missing operation that never makes the state observable. The three lines of work below each report one total.

Video generators as world models.  Large video generators are treated as simulators or interactive environments (Brooks et al., 2024; Bruce and others, 2024; Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a). Long-horizon systems add packing, retrieval, or persistent state to reduce drift (Henschel et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c). Neither line shows that a hidden state was kept and updated.

Hidden state and stage-resolved evaluation.  A hidden state cannot be scored if the requested update never happens. StEvo-Bench, MemoBench, and the Video Shell Game study updates under occlusion or unseen swaps (Shin et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). WRBench and MBench add a camera leave and a later check (Lu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Temporal and physical suites likewise separate whether a transition occurs from whether its endpoint is correct (Feng et al., 2024; Bansal et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). MIST applies that principle to delayed reveal; it does not replace Official WRBench, Official MBench, or the Video Shell Game.

Judges and test-time refinement.  Structured VLM judges help on appearance, but remain weakest on temporal and motion errors (Tong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025b). VideoRepair, PhyT2V, Video-T1, and VQQA already diagnose or rewrite videos for quality, physics, or preference (Lee et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2026), but none asks whether the asked change was shown. M3-Agent instead revises the instruction so the model carries that change out. We claim no numbered comparison with the tools above. The broader map is in Appendix B.

3 MIST: separating scene setup from delayed state reveal

The cases in Fig. 2 show a missing final state, but not why it is missing. A closed lid and a change that was never carried out can produce the same total. MIST separates the two (Fig. 3a). The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it.

What the evaluation does.  A delayed query asks who sits where, what is inside, or how many objects remain. In text, this is a question about a target state sT⋆s_{T}^{\star}. For a video generator, the clip must also produce that state on screen. MIST names sT⋆s_{T}^{\star}, hides it behind an opaque gap, and only then asks the generator to show it. Each case is three 5-second shots: the first establishes the scene, the second passes through the opaque gap, and the third requests the reveal. All reveal comparisons reuse the same locked first two shots. The baseline prompt and the gap never contain the answer; the ablations that do name it are marked as such. The paired reveal analysis freezes the first two shots and regenerates only the last shot from the same pre-reveal context. Answer-only and diagnosis-guided arms may place the target in the reveal prompt; Table 3 marks that access. A prompt-channel audit confirms the target in the M3 and same-sentence templates and confirms its removal from the generic open-and-hold arm, so that arm is answer-free. The same-sentence resample is an equal-compute control, not a target-free control. R0–R2 cover presence and count, binding, and history-update operations (Table 1).

Three observable gates.  Let x1:T=G(π,c)x_{1:T}=G(\pi,c) denote a clip from a frozen generator GG (Team Wan, 2025), prompt π\pi, and image or caption context cc, and let JJ be a fixed VLM judge (Liu et al., 2023a; Tong et al., 2024). We distinguish whether the required move occurs (IactI_{\mathrm{act}}), whether the last frame is readable (IvisI_{\mathrm{vis}}), and whether that frame matches the target (match⁡(x,sT⋆)=J⁡(xT,sT⋆)\mathrm{match}(x,s_{T}^{\star})=J(x_{T},s_{T}^{\star})). A score that requires all three is

score⁡(x,sT⋆)=Iact​(x)⋅Ivis​(x)⋅match⁡(x,sT⋆).\mathrm{score}(x,s_{T}^{\star})\;=\;I_{\mathrm{act}}(x)\cdot I_{\mathrm{vis}}(x)\cdot\mathrm{match}(x,s_{T}^{\star}). (1)

Eq. (1) says that a total collapses when any factor is missing, and the total alone cannot tell a missing action from an incorrect state. We therefore report the factors separately rather than their product (Fig. 3a): setup checks the first shot, leak the gap, and reveal and inside the last shot. Never-open is the thresholded action class, not the mean reveal: a low mean is not a never-open count (Figure 6). A valid setup followed by a closed lid places the failure on the reveal path, not on forgetting.

WRBench and MBench-T test the same gates in one continuous clip. Each publishes a unique score, TT and UU, that gives no credit when a step of this path is missing:

a→leave​until unjudgeable→return→hold⁡(xT),a\;\to\;\mathrm{leave}\;\text{until unjudgeable}\;\to\;\mathrm{return}\;\to\;\mathrm{hold}(x_{T}), (2)

where aa is the requested event, such as a sit or a break. The score thus requires the executed move, not only a final match (§7).

4 Pre-experiments: the target is named, but the reveal is missing

We apply the MIST measures before designing an agent or evaluating an official suite. Two questions come first. At which gate does the baseline fail, and can naming the target fix it?

Does the scene fail before memory is tested?  Setup is high (Table 2): in most first shots the objects and the container are in place. In 38 of 43 cases setup is at least 0.8 while the baseline reveal stays below 0.3. What is missing is the later move that shows the asked-for state.

Where does the baseline fail?  Mean reveal stays low. When each clip receives one label, 41 of 43 baseline clips never open; one opens to an empty or blocked view, and one is correct. In the closed cases the final state cannot be evaluated at all, because the required action never exposes it. On those 41 clips, a hand comes in and does not open in 38, nobody comes in in 3, and the wrong object is opened in none. The shot length is not why the lid stays down (Figure 6), but the three-shot stitch shapes how the failure looks: on a packed 15s MiniMax-H3 take the same judge finds 3 of 43 never-open and 24 of 43 opened onto the wrong state (Appendix C). The failure moves from not opening to opening wrong; in both cases the asked change is not carried out. A low total here says nothing about whether the model forgot sT⋆s_{T}^{\star}: persistence has not been tested yet.

Did the hidden gap leak the answer?  No target is visible in the middle chunk. Paired gap leak is 0/430/43 for both the baseline and the later rewrite. A broader 51-row baseline export also contains no leak, but that export is not the paired denominator. Setup is not a leak. The reveal failure does not follow an early exposure of the answer; it occurs at the action gate in Eq. (1).

What changes after a targeted rewrite?  We inspect the last shot, diagnose its failed move, and rewrite only that shot. With one kept clip per case, rather than best-of-five, reveal rises and inside match rises with it (Table 2). Setup remains flat. Per case, reveal rises in 35 of 43, stays the same in 6, and falls in 2; the mean paired change is 0.34 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.45). The failure class also changes. Of the baseline never-opens, rewrite leaves many closed, opens some onto a wrong state, and makes some correct (Fig. 4a). The table’s open-but-wrong clips include newly opened wrong states plus the initially correct case R2-10, which the rewrite can break. The rewrite exposes more states, but it does not guarantee that the exposed state is correct. Accounting detail is in Figure 6.

All three operation families move the same way, and setup stays flat in each: reveal goes from 0.132 to 0.549 on presence and count, from 0.147 to 0.464 on binding, and from 0.163 to 0.454 on a history update (Fig. 4c; Figure 6). Closed lids that remain are not piled in one family. Openings onto the wrong state are failed updates, not noise in one family (Figure 6). The rewrite has to spell out both the move and the last-frame evidence, not only a verb.

Is naming the target enough?  The kept-clip diagnosis above locates the failure at the reveal gate; it does not yet explain what kind of instruction opens that gate. If the missing piece were only the answer, inserting sT⋆s_{T}^{\star} should suffice. If it were only a verb, “open and hold” should suffice. We allocate the same five tries in five ways (Table 3, Fig. 4): the answer sentence is present or absent, and the failed move is either rewritten or left unchanged. A fifth arm rewrites the move from the same last frame but forbids every target noun, color, and count (audited; 0/43 leaks).

The ordering in Table 3 separates these explanations. The bare “open and hold” instruction performs worst. Supplying the answer helps, but resampling the same sentence does not match a diagnosis-guided rewrite. Looking at the clip and changing the failed move gives the strongest best-of-five reveal and inside scores (0.763 against 0.684 for answer-only). With the target withheld the same rewrite reaches 0.174 and leaves 28 of 43 lids closed: on this probe the rewrite opens the lid only when the prompt also says what is inside. Each arm keeps, per case, the try whose last frame the judge scores highest, so no cell here is the one-clip mean of Table 2. Later tries are not better on average, so the best-of-five cell is a running best (Fig. 4d). Where the same cases have an unchanged-prompt control, extra draws of the same sentence do not explain the gain. The running best moves most between the second and third try, from 0.546 to 0.700, and the last two tries add little. On six cases with a matched resample, the same-prompt running best is 0.4100.410, 0.5570.557, 0.5610.561, 0.5700.570, 0.5800.580, while the rewritten move on those same cases reaches 0.8840.884. Constraints-only and ledger-only reach 0.1890.189 and 0.2150.215 on that subset. The subset is too small to replace the 43-case table. The pass-by-pass record behind Fig. 4d is in Table 9: per-pass means are not monotone, and “inside of chosen” is not the kept-clip inside match 0.4420.442.

The same missing operation appears on an Internal MiniMax-H3 take (Fig. 3): the raw take puts a different object in the tin and opens to it; the rewritten instruction puts the orange marble and opens to that. Clip settings and cell boundaries are in Appendix C.

Asking only to open fails, naming the target helps, and revising the failed move helps most, but only with the target named. The next section turns look, diagnose, and change into a test-time workflow.

5 M3-Agent: revise the instruction for the missing change

The pre-experiments show that the workflow must revise the failed instruction, not append the target or repeat the same prompt. M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move) does that at test time (Fig. 3b): it reads the last frame, revises the details of the instruction for that change, and generates again with the same model. It does not add or train a memory module.

The workflow has three steps. First, a short task record lists the actor or object, its required binding, the operation, and the evidence that must appear in xTx_{T}; these fields come from the task card. Second, a VLM inspects the generated last frame against that record and assigns a visible failure mode, such as no action, wrong binding, missing departure, return to an intact object, or an occluded view. Third, the workflow rewrites the failed operation rather than the answer, and the frozen generator produces another candidate. This third step is the one that works in Table 3. The rewrite preserves the actor, object, target state, and temporal order; only the failed operation and its final-frame evidence clause may change. Diagnosis reads the rendered xTx_{T} once, never the generator’s hidden states.

A worked case.  Figure 3b traces the workflow on that case. The task record asks for the orange marble in the tin, the purple disk outside, and a visible marble at the end. The raw take opens the tin onto another object, which the record labels a wrong binding rather than a missing action. The revised instruction keeps the tin, the disk, and the order of events, and names the object that must go in; the next take opens onto the orange marble. The raw take stays in the candidate set, so a revision that makes things worse is not kept.

Given KK candidates, M3-Agent keeps the clip that best carries out the instruction,

x^=arg⁡maxk≤K​score​(x(k),sT⋆),\hat{x}\;=\;\underset{k\leq K}{\arg\max}\;\mathrm{score}\!\left(x^{(k)},s_{T}^{\star}\right), (3)

and the original candidate remains in the set. The score here is the same check that reports the result: the MIST judge on MIST, and the official gates on WRBench and MBench-T. A reader that sees only the last frame, without that score, does not reliably beat the baseline (§8). A single revision is not always better: R2-10, for example, turns a correct case into an incorrect one, so the original clip stays eligible. Searching several instructions at test time is a known strategy (Snell et al., 2024; Oshima et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Khalaf et al., 2025; Landesberg, 2026). Every reported best-of-KK and official keep-best cell is chosen after generation with the reporting scorer; that is an oracle coverage estimate, not a deployable critic (Appendix A).

On MIST.  The agent works with frozen TI2V-5B. It preserves the first two 5-second shots and rewrites only the final reveal shot, and the reveal prompt may include sT⋆s_{T}^{\star} (Table 3). The kept-clip analysis in Table 2 locks one outcome per case; Table 3 instead generates K=5K{=}5 candidates per arm and applies Eq. (3).

On WRBench and MBench-T.  The agent works on 10-second clips from frozen T2V-A14B and keeps each suite’s official camera clause; on WRBench the caption stays task-context none. Candidate instructions establish the requested relation before departure and hold it after return. On MBench-T the candidate set must include the original clip: forcing another leave–return can preserve the camera motion while worsening the returned state. Selection is made per sample over a small instruction set.

6 Evaluation setup

We never merge numbers from different scorers. Every number below is Official (the suite’s own scorer) or Internal (our fixed judge). Adapted protocols are not pooled with these rows. The three-chunk MBench condition is omitted. Main claims use Wan TI2V-5B for Internal MIST, Wan T2V-A14B for Official WRBench and MBench-T, and MiniMax-H3 as an Internal qualitative pilot (Fig. 3; Appendix C). Clip lengths, seeds, judges, and budgets are in Tables 7, 8, 9 and 10. Internal and Official exports keep separate manifests and are never pooled.

7 Main results: the same diagnosis on official scores

Under the scorers fixed in §6, we ask whether official memory protocols fail at the same execution gates isolated by MIST. Inspecting failed clips on official WRBench and MBench-T shows the same missing action. The analysis transfers a diagnosis, not a number: Internal MIST, Official unique scores, and packed H3 pilots remain separate cells (Appendix C).

What do the official scores contain?  Both suites already require the path in Eq. (2) (Lu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). We report which gates change and which clip is kept per item. We do not treat a correlation between a total and one of its own parts as a separate causal finding (Appendix A).

What happens when we search that path?  The two official protocols fail at different points, and those points map onto the two remaining MIST failure types. On WRBench, the camera often does not complete the required departure and return: a shut D​6D6 gate is the same class as a never-open, so persistence is not yet measured. On MBench-T the camera returns, but the object is often still intact (Fig. 2): the path completed, yet the aftermath is the wrong world state, as in the open-but-wrong MIST clips. The search therefore has two different jobs. On WRBench it has to find a missing path. On MBench-T it has to keep the original clip when a fixed rewrite harms the aftermath.

On WRBench, score TT rises (Table 5) because the camera finishes the return, not because the frame looks better. The paired gain has a 95% bootstrap interval of +0.070+0.070 to +0.166+0.166 (Appendix A). The component audit attributes about 3–4% of Δ​T\Delta T to visual quality, 55–56% to the departure check D​5′D5^{\prime}, and 41% to the return check D​6′D6^{\prime}, depending on rounding (Fig. 5a). Of the 40 return gates, 18 stay open, 13 newly open, none close, and 9 stay shut (Fig. 5b). A second instruction set can lower the total, from 0.5500.550 to 0.5470.547; the last step restores it to 0.5700.570. Adding a skill is therefore not monotone. Table 10 places the kept result next to two ceilings that are not the method: a peek at the gate followed by visual selection reaches 0.5860.586, and the maximum TT in the pack is 0.6010.601. The reported method is the unique-head result T=0.570T{=}0.570.

On MBench-T the camera already comes back, so UU follows the state after return, not whether the camera left (Table 4). Fourteen of 30 cases stay hard: the leave–return trigger usually fires, but the object comes back unchanged or wrong, and a prompt that only says to hold the update fixes none of those 14. Fixed leave–return hurts 8 cases whose baseline state score is 1.0. A last-frame lock, used as the only clip, gives U=0.228U=0.228; it helps the pack only because selection may refuse it. A later destroy-and-hold instruction stays near the floor as a fixed arm and flips one additional case only under oracle selection. That cell is not a headline method. Selection keeps the baseline on 23 items, the leave–return instruction on 5, and the last-frame lock on 2 (Fig. 5c). The published 0.4460.446 averages a state pick and a correctness pick. One clip per item gives 0.4430.443. Trigger versus conditional scores are in Table 11; they are not MIST metrics.

What do the ablations constrain?  Table 3 rules out answer text or unchanged resampling as the sole explanation for the MIST rewrite. The official ablations add two boundaries. On MBench-T, a prompt that only asks to hold the update does not fix the hard cases, and a last-frame lock alone is worse than the baseline (Table 4). On WRBench, the best-looking clip and the clip kept for TT are different clips (Table 5), so a readable frame is not the executed path. Score-composition plots are in Figure 6.

Can the judge answer without the video?  A text-only control separates a text shortcut from visual evidence (Table 6). A held-out 8B reader names gold sT⋆s_{T}^{\star} from text, then collapses when the gold sentence is removed or shuffled. On the locked last frame it tracks the 122B inside check: almost no baseline clip is accepted, and the rewrite rate matches Table 2. Naming the target is easy; seeing the executed state is not. Agreement with official gates is much lower (Appendix D); the reread does not replace either official scorer (Han et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025c; Chen et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2026).

8 Discussion: what execution evidence can establish

MIST separates the scene, the change, and the last frame (Eqs. (1)–(2)); M3-Agent revises the instruction. Neither shows what the model stored.

Measurement.  A high reveal is not a memory claim. If the asked change never occurs, persistence is untested, whether the clip stays closed or opens onto the wrong state (Table 2; §4).

Selection.  Keep-best is an oracle over a small candidate pool, scored by the same check that reports the result. The rewrite may name the target, and a target-withheld control fails (Table 3). A last-frame reader that does not see the score does not beat the baseline (Table 12). Because a rewrite can damage a correct case, the original clip stays eligible.

Scope.  The main study uses one generator family under Internal and Official protocols; packed MiniMax-H3 cells stay Internal (Fig. 3; Appendix C). The held-out judge check is not human validation (Appendix D). Claim boundaries are in Table 13.

What a positive result would need.  We cannot claim the backbone stored sT⋆s_{T}^{\star}. That claim would need a target-blind selector that beats the baseline, held-out cases, and human labels on the exposed state. Until then, an opened lid shows that the state can be judged, not that it was remembered.

9 Conclusion

MIST splits one memory score into three questions: was the scene set, was the asked change carried out, and does the last frame show the result. On the Internal cases the scene and gap usually hold, yet the baseline often never shows the change, so persistence is not yet tested. Revising the failed instruction exposes more of the target state than naming it alone, though the shown state can still be wrong.

M3-Agent revises the instruction so the same frozen model carries out the change. Relative to the baseline, reveal rises on Internal MIST and the Official unique scores improve, with opposite keep-best consequences on the two suites. These cells do not establish that the backbone stored sT⋆s_{T}^{\star}. A memory evaluation should publish the three checks apart, not one total.

Appendix A Protocol cards and budgets

Table 7 lists the settings behind the main claims. H3 packed-15s pilots are a fourth Internal cell, not a fourth official track (Appendix C). Table 8 expands each track.

MIST uses Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, three 5-second shots, and seed class 9042. The 122B judge reads six positions in the reveal shot, {0.90,0.93,0.95,0.97,0.99,0.995}\{0.90,0.93,0.95,0.97,0.99,0.995\}. Its prompt and parsing stay frozen across arms. Paired intervals use 4,000 bootstrap resamples over the 43 cases with seed 0; the paired Wilcoxon test uses the same pairs. Official WRBench uses Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, 161 frames over 10 seconds, yaw_LR, task-context none, and the released scorer. Official MBench-T uses the same generator and duration, five native caption segments, and the released causal metrics. These settings differ jointly from MIST, so TI2V-5B versus T2V-A14B is not a controlled comparison of model scale.

Appendix B Extended literature map and positioning

This section records the wider 2024–2026 literature used to bound the paper’s claims. Entries are grouped by the question they answer, rather than presented as evidence for one aggregate notion of “memory.”

What enables long and persistent rollouts?  Diffusion and latent-video foundations establish the rendering lineage [Ho et al., 2020, Blattmann et al., 2023, Team Wan, 2025], while physical-AI platforms broaden the world-model framing [NVIDIA et al., 2025]. Recent systems address exposure bias, out-of-sight dynamics, bounded memory, and revisit stability through self-conditioned training or explicit state [Huang et al., 2025b, Duan et al., 2026b, Team et al., 2026, Xu et al., 2026b]. Omnimodal enterable worlds, controlled action-memory probes, and long-horizon audio–visual story generation extend the same line [Zhang et al., 2026b, King et al., 2026, Duan et al., 2026a]. Agent-driven and embodied evaluations further test whether action-conditioned worlds remain usable over long objectives [Ding et al., 2026, Wang and Li, 2026, Yang et al., 2026, Liu et al., 2026]. EntityBench separately measures recurring entities across multi-shot gaps [He et al., 2026b]. Long-horizon generators and packing systems also appear in the main related work [Wu et al., 2024b, Xiang et al., 2024, Zhu et al., 2024, Garcin et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026]. These works motivate long-horizon memory, but architectural success in one protocol does not resolve MIST’s execution-versus-persistence ambiguity.

Which benchmark dimensions are adjacent to MIST?  WorldBench and IntPhys 2 isolate physical concepts and object permanence, whereas EWMBench and VBench 2.0 separate scene, motion, semantics, and intrinsic faithfulness [Upadhyay et al., 2026, Bordes et al., 2025, Yue et al., 2025, Zheng et al., 2025]. Understanding suites separate endpoint answers from continuous tracking [Yu et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026b, Han et al., 2026b]. LongVideoBench and MLVU test long-context understanding rather than generator-side state production [Wu et al., 2024a, Zhou et al., 2024]. ChronoMagic-Bench separates amount of change from temporal coherence, and T2VPhysBench evaluates physical laws with manual judgments [Yuan et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2025]. Adjacent temporal and physical suites include TC-Bench, T2V-CompBench, OSC-Bench, YoCausal, PhyGenBench, and VideoPhy2 [Sun et al., 2024, Han et al., 2026a, Xie et al., 2026, Meng et al., 2024, Bansal et al., 2025]. MIST instead fixes a target state and asks whether the generated operation makes that state judgeable after an opaque gap.

How has video generation been refined at test time?  Reward gradients and human-feedback rewards improve video generation through learned objectives [Prabhudesai et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2025b]. GenMAC and Prompt-A-Video use collaborative or preference-aligned prompt revision [Huang et al., 2024, Ji et al., 2024]. ScalingNoise, VISTA, RAPO++, and ImagerySearch broaden search over noise, prompts, candidates, or evaluators [Yang et al., 2025a, Long et al., 2025, Gao et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2025]. LatSearch and noise-trajectory search move selection inside diffusion inference, while GEARS diagnoses and recycles candidates [Zhao et al., 2026, Ramesh and Mardani, 2025, He et al., 2026a]. M3-Agent is not a generic test-time search. Its contribution is an operation-constrained response to a delayed-reveal diagnosis, and its score-aware selection remains an oracle coverage analysis.

What can automated video evaluators establish?  VBench and EvalCrafter established multidimensional evaluation beyond single perceptual totals [Huang et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023b]. VideoScore, AIGV-Assessor, LOVE, and UVE learn or organize fine-grained human-facing quality or task judgments [He et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025c, Li et al., 2024]. VideoGen-Eval decomposes prompts into checkable questions, while WorldJen and RAVEN-Eval study rubric design, score compression, ordering, and confidence [Yang et al., 2025b, Inbasekar et al., 2026, Jia et al., 2026]. CLIP-style alignment and vision-centric VLMs provide useful readers [Radford et al., 2021, Liu et al., 2023a, Tong et al., 2024], but no one reader is treated here as ground truth for latent state. This is why MIST reports gate-specific judgments, a held-out reread, and explicit disagreement with official scorers. Embedding-centric vision learners and generators, and cycle-consistent text-guided image editing, sit adjacent to the representation and prompt-revision tools used above [Xu et al., 2025, Xu et al., 2026a, Xu et al., 2023].

Appendix C Other generations of the same cards

The MIST cards name the same objects and operations throughout. The experiments do not. Table 14 lists the generator, the duration, the judge, and the claim for each reported cell. Headline MIST is Wan TI2V-5B, three 5-second shots, and the locked 122B judge. Official WRBench and MBench-T are Wan A14B, 10 seconds, and the released scorers. MiniMax-H3 pilots are packed 15s Internal takes. A number from one row is not evidence for another row. The strip in Fig. 3 is the Internal MiniMax-H3 packed take of R0-03: not the Wan TI2V-5B n=43n{=}43 stitch, not the equal-budget comparison in Table 3, and not Official TT/UU.

A packed 15s take fails differently from the stitch.  The headline 41/4341/43 never-open rate is a Wan TI2V-5B stitch of three 5-second shots. The same 43 cards can be packed into one MiniMax-H3 15s take: T2VA, short edge 768, seed 61001. The raw prompt does not include the last-frame state sentence; the M3 arm adds that sentence. Prompt expansion is not used in this 43-case run. Table 15 applies the locked 122B reveal judge, with the same prompt and positions as Table 2. The raw take opens in 40 of 43 cases. Its failure is a wrong exposed state (24/43), not a closed lid. The never-open cell is therefore a property of the stitch, not a property of every generator. These are Internal packed cells, one clip per arm, with no keep-best. They are not Official TT or UU, and they are not the population of Table 2.

Continuity asks only whether the 15s take hard-cuts. A frame pair fails when the gray-frame mean absolute error is at least 22. Table 16 is not a memory score, and 0.605→0.7210.605\rightarrow 0.721 is not reveal and not Official TT or UU. M3 raises the pass rate and is not monotone: 12 cases fail raw and pass M3, while 7 pass raw and fail M3. Both arms pass on 19 of 43 (Table 17).

A six-case pilot is not a scale result.  Table 18 uses an Internal 8B judge on six cards. H3 and Lingbot are separate generation pipelines. Neither uses an official memory protocol. The arms are mixed rather than monotone: H3 prompt expansion lowers the middle-shot score while raising reveal, stacking M3 and expansion is worse than either arm alone, and Lingbot stays near the floor. The diagnose-and-rewrite workflow can be run as a packed 15s prompt on MiniMax-H3. That does not support a claim about scale or about an official protocol. The planned 12-case H3 expansion was paused before scoring. Lingbot M3 arms were not run. We also do not fill in cells that were not run: a VideoRepair or Video-T1 comparison at K=5K{=}5 (the released Video-T1 code drives Pyramid-Flow, not Wan, and was not ported), or human labels on the 43 last frames.

Figure 7 keeps the stills that this distinction depends on. Panels (a–d) are one still pack. Panels (e–f) are the seed-61001 run. The packs are not the same files: R0-02 passes the continuity harness in the still pack and fails it in the 43-case run. Panel (a) is the R0-03 take in Fig. 3. Panel (d), R2-12, fails the harness in both arms, and the last frame shows the wrong object.

Internal rescores and runs that produced no clips.  Table 19 rescores some of the same videos with a different judge. Official TT and Official UU stay the rows already reported. The Internal reveal on WRBench, 0.372→0.6680.372\rightarrow 0.668, and the Internal unique score on a 12-case MBench-T slice, 0.230→0.4260.230\rightarrow 0.426, use a different scale. They are not added to TT or UU. A scored intermediate pack at 0.4630.463 is not an official cell and is not a claim of this paper. Official UU remains 0.4460.446.

One further protocol was attempted and did not yield a score. It paired TI2V-5B aftermath stills with an A14B image-to-video stitch of 161 frames, seed 10042, on 12 items, instead of frozen T2V-A14B. The run failed before producing clips (FSDP no_sync; 0/12), so it has no official score. Adapted MemoBench and SANA-WM smoke tests are excluded for the same reason: their generation or metrics are not the protocol in Table 8.

Appendix D Held-out last-frame judge

The main 122B judge is unchanged. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct rereads the same locked last frames as Table 6 and answers YES or NO to sT⋆s_{T}^{\star}. Official TT and UU are not replaced. The main-text last-frame rate 0.0230.023 is a strict YES rate. Mean inside in Table 2 is 0.0470.047. Agreement with the 122B inside check is high on the baseline because almost every baseline frame is negative. Agreement on the action bit of rewritten frames is much lower, and agreement with official WRBench and MBench gates is lower still (Table 20). An 8B YES is not an official D​5D5 or D​6D6 decision, and it is not an MBench state score. Those rubrics ask different questions.
